title: Shimon ben Azzai
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: Ben Azzai is mentioned in the Mishnah much more often than his colleague Ben Zoma. In Berakhot 9:4 he says that one entering a city says four prayers, two on entering and two on leaving. At the beginning of Shekalim 3 he disagrees with Rabbi Akiva about the dates on which the chamber's funds are withdrawn. In 4:6 he tells Rabbi Akiva that the cases are not comparable. At 5:3 he says that there were five seals in the Temple. In Yoma 2:3 he tells Rabbi Akiva in Rabbi Yehoshua's name that the offering was brought up in the order in which the animal walked. In Taanit 4:4 he reports to Rabbi Akiva how Rabbi Yehoshua taught the case of the additional offering. Rabbi Akiva then changed his teaching to agree with Ben Azzai.[^1]

In Yevamot 4:13 Shimon ben Azzai says that he found a genealogical scroll in Jerusalem recording that a certain person was a mamzer born of a married woman, in support of Rabbi Yehoshua's position. The baraita in Yevamot 49b also records from that scroll that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's Mishnah is scant but pure, and that Manasseh killed Isaiah. In Sotah 3:4 Ben Azzai derives that a man must teach his daughter Torah so that, if she drinks the ordeal water, she will know that merit can delay its effect. Hyman contrasts this with Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua.

In Bava Batra 9:10 Ben Azzai tells Rabbi Akiva that they already regret the disputed cases and that Akiva has come to dispute even the agreed cases. In Horayot 1:2 he asks Rabbi Akiva how this person differs from someone who stayed at home. In Zevachim 1:2 he reports a tradition from the seventy-two elders on the day Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah was seated in the academy concerning sacrifices. Ben Azzai added only the burnt offering, and the sages did not agree with him. In Yadayim 3:5 he likewise reports a tradition from the seventy-two elders that Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes render the hands impure. Rabbi Akiva protests. Rabbi Yochanan ben Yehoshua, son of Rabbi Akiva's father-in-law, says that the disagreement and its resolution were as Ben Azzai stated.

In Bekhorot 9:5 he disagrees with Rabbi Akiva about the times for tithing animals. In Kinnim 2:5 he follows the first offering, and in 3:6 he rules that there are two sin offerings. At the beginning of Parah, Rabbi Yehoshua reports what he heard without explanation and Ben Azzai offers to explain it. In Parah 1:3 Rabbi Tarfon calls the animal a palges, Ben Azzai calls it a noked, and Rabbi Yishmael gives another name. In Niddah 5:8, alongside the opinions of Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva, Ben Azzai identifies the sign as the darkening of the nipple.

Hyman infers that Rabbi Yehoshua was among Ben Azzai's teachers from the teachings he reports to Rabbi Akiva in Yoma and Taanit, his support for Rabbi Yehoshua in Yevamot 4:13, and his explanations of Rabbi Yehoshua in Parah and Tosefta Sheviit chapter 2. Hyman calls Rabbi Akiva his principal teacher. In Bava Batra 158b Rabbi Simlai infers from Ben Azzai's wording “you have come” that he was Rabbi Akiva's pupil and colleague. Rashbam explains that he was first his pupil and later his colleague. Rabbenu Gershom describes the two going to study under Rabbi Eliezer the Great. Ben Azzai was young and could not match Akiva's reasoning. He learned the received teaching and later came to Akiva for the reasoning. Hyman proposes that the text of Rabbenu Gershom should name Rabbi Yehoshua, from whom Ben Azzai does transmit teachings, rather than Rabbi Eliezer, from whom Hyman finds none.[^2]

In Berakhot 62a Ben Azzai says that he followed Rabbi Akiva into the privy and learned three things. Rabbi Yehudah asks how he dared take such liberties with his teacher. Ben Azzai similarly asks Rabbi Akiva how he dared take such liberties with his teacher when Akiva tells of following Rabbi Yehoshua. Hyman explains that calling someone “your teacher” in this exchange need not imply that the speaker did not also learn from him. In Mekhilta, Bo 1, and Sifra, Vayikra 2, Shimon ben Azzai says that he is adding to, rather than objecting to, the words of his teacher, whom Hyman identifies as Rabbi Akiva. In Berakhot 22a Rabbi Akiva whispers a teaching to Ben Azzai.

Ketubot 63a says that Rabbi Akiva's daughter did for Ben Azzai as her mother had done for Akiva. Hyman explains that she betrothed herself to him in secret on condition that he go to study. As the popular saying has it, the ewe follows the ewe, and the daughter follows her mother's ways. Sotah 4b gives the possibility that he married and separated. Hyman connects his separation from ordinary worldly life with his devotion to Torah and his entry into the pardes. In Yevamot 63b Ben Azzai teaches that failing to engage in procreation is like shedding blood and diminishing the divine image. When challenged that he teaches well but does not practice what he teaches, he answers that his soul longs for Torah and that others can sustain the world. Hyman conjectures that after divorcing Rabbi Akiva's daughter he parted from Rabbi Akiva as well, and later regretted not attending him longer, as in Nedarim 74b. He likewise regretted not attending Rabbi Yishmael, as in Chullin 70b–71a.[^3]

Ben Azzai continued to acknowledge Rabbi Akiva's greatness. In Bekhorot 58a he compares all the sages of Israel to garlic peel in his eyes except “this bald man,” whom Rashi identifies as Rabbi Akiva. He was among the four called “those who deliberate before the sages,” with Shimon ben Zoma, Chanan the Egyptian, and Chananyah ben Chakhinai, as in Sanhedrin 17b. In Horayot 2b Rava gives Ben Azzai and Ben Zoma as examples of those fit to rule. In Kiddushin 49b one who stipulates that he is a student need not be a student on their level. Rashi explains that they were young students who had not reached ordination and that none of their contemporaries equaled them in Torah.[^4]

Among Ben Azzai's legal teachings in baraitot, Hyman cites the juxtaposition from which he derives stoning for a sorceress in Berakhot 21b. He treats walking as equivalent to standing in the discussion of carrying, passing, and throwing on Shabbat. In Rosh Hashanah 6a he distinguishes the offering itself, which may fail to be accepted, from the consequences of delaying a vow. In Yevamot 51b he holds that a second levirate declaration after a first can take effect when there are two brothers. In Sotah he measures the duration of seclusion by the time to roast an egg, among several differing measures. In Kiddushin 25a, Rabbi includes castration and Ben Azzai includes the tongue. The Talmud explains that Chana heard and fixed Rabbi's teaching first and then taught Ben Azzai's, and the Mishnah's arrangement was retained. In Bava Kamma 84b Rabbi says the burn was stated first, and Ben Azzai says the wound was stated first. In 105a he distinguishes three oaths. Hyman also cites Mekhilta, Bo 18, Beshalach 1, and Mishpatim 10.[^5]

In Avot 4:2–3 Ben Azzai urges one to run to a minor mitzvah as to a major one and to flee transgression, since a mitzvah leads to another mitzvah. He also urges one not to despise any person or dismiss any thing, for every person has an hour and every thing a place. At the end of Avot deRabbi Natan 25 he advises sitting two or three places below one's station, so that one may be invited up rather than told to go down. He would rather rule the world than sit and teach before people wrapped in sheets, which Hyman takes to mean people whose inner character does not match their outward appearance. Hyman cites Vayikra Rabbah 1:5 and proposes correcting its transmission formula to read Rabbi Akiva, with another version attributing the saying to Rabbi Shimon ben Azzai.

In Berakhot 6b Ben Azzai explains “for this is the whole of man” as meaning that the world was created to accompany the person who fears Heaven. At 47a he says that one who prolongs the response amen has his days and years prolonged. At 47b he defines an am haaretz as someone without fringes on his garment. In Yoma 38a he teaches that you will be called by your own name, seated in your own place, and given what is yours. No one can touch what is destined for another, and no reign encroaches on another by even a hairbreadth. Hyman speculates that Ben Azzai said this because he had not received ordination and took the matter as a decree of Heaven and an expression of providence.

In Megillah 13a he describes Esther as neither tall nor short but of middling stature, like a myrtle. In Menachot 110a he teaches that whether one gives much or little, what matters is directing one's heart toward Heaven. In Torat Kohanim on “Love your fellow as yourself,” Rabbi Akiva calls this a great principle of the Torah. Ben Azzai calls “This is the book of the generations of Adam” a greater principle. Hyman also points to Yerushalmi Nedarim 9:3. In Arakhin 16b Ben Azzai says that rebuke continues until a sharp reprimand, differing from Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua. Vayikra Rabbah 16:4 tells that fire blazed around him as he taught. Asked whether he was expounding the Chariot, he says he was stringing together words of Torah with the Prophets, and the Prophets with the Writings.[^6]

Hyman takes Ben Azzai's explanation of hadar as idur in Sukkah 35a as evidence of his knowledge of Greek. Among his practical sayings in Berakhot 62b are to lie on any bed except the ground, sit on any seat except a beam, and go out early and late to relieve oneself. Hyman describes Rabbi Yose HaGelili as something of a colleague. In Sifra, Metzora, at Hyman's locator 152, Rabbi Yose HaGelili asks him to explain and Ben Azzai answers that one does not explain to a sage. Hyman cites disagreements in Nedarim 78a and Bava Kamma 13a.

Hyman places his regular seat in Tiberias. In Eruvin 29a Rava declares himself like Ben Azzai in the markets of Tiberias, and in Kiddushin 20a Abaye does likewise. In Yerushalmi Bikkurim 2:2 Rabbi Yochanan, whom Hyman places in Tiberias, declares himself the Ben Azzai of that place. Hyman infers that Ben Azzai taught many pupils there from Berakhot 22a, where Rabbi Akiva whispers a teaching and Ben Azzai goes out and teaches it to his pupils in the market. Their names are not given, but in Temurah 21b Rabbi Yose reports three matters in the names of three elders, Rabbi Yishmael, Rabbi Akiva, and Ben Azzai.

In Bava Kamma 59a, where Rabbi Yose deducts the midwife's fee and Ben Azzai deducts the cost of food, Hyman proposes reading Rabbi Yose HaGelili for Rabbi Yose. He also explains the report in Nazir 65a from Rabbi Yochanan in Ben Azzai's name as referring to the tanna quoted in the baraita there on how much surrounding earth is removed with a corpse.

Beyond his Torah learning, Hyman describes Ben Azzai as studying the mysteries of the Chariot and Creation. In Chagigah 14b four entered the pardes, Ben Azzai, Ben Zoma, Acher, and Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Akiva warned them not to cry “water, water” upon reaching the stones of pure marble. Rabbi Akiva entered and left in peace, but Ben Azzai looked and died, of whom Scripture says that the death of God's faithful is precious in His eyes. Ben Zoma looked and was harmed. Hyman reports the reverse in the Yerushalmi. Rashi says Ben Azzai died young, while Hyman infers that he reached old age. He already ranked among the sages deliberating at Yavneh and lived to speak as a colleague with Rabbi Yehudah, citing Berakhot 62a and Yevamot 4a. In Chullin 7b Rabbi Yonatan, who served Rabbi Yishmael near the end of his life, says that he spoke with Ben Azzai, who asked him what Yishmael had said.[^7]

Midrash Tehillim 9:13 and Eichah Rabbah 2, on “He swallowed up,” count Ben Azzai among those executed by the government. Hyman takes the Mishnah at the end of Sotah, “When Ben Azzai died, the diligent ceased,” and the account in Chagigah that he looked and died, as suggesting a death in the ordinary course. Berakhot 57b says that one who sees Ben Azzai in a dream may look forward to piety.

notes.text: This is Hyman’s full article under Shimon ben Azzai. His separate Ben Azzai heading directs readers to this entry. The translation follows the Wikisource witness, retaining Hyman’s abridgments and proposals. His second reference to Taanit gives chapter 2, whereas his earlier reference gives 4:4.

Bava Batra 158b explicitly describes Ben Azzai as Rabbi Akiva’s pupil and colleague. The cited Rabbi Yehoshua traditions do not identify him as Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha. Hyman’s proposed correction to Rabbenu Gershom is a conjecture.

Ketubot 63a gives the parallel with Akiva’s wife. Sotah 4b offers marriage followed by separation as one of several explanations. Yevamot 63b preserves Ben Azzai’s answer about his devotion to Torah. Hyman’s reconstruction of divorce and its effect on his studies goes beyond those texts.

Bekhorot 58a leaves “this bald man” unnamed. Rashi identifies him as Akiva, while Tosafot report a different identification from Rabbenu Nissim. See Hyman’s Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha entry for the separate dispute over paternity.

The supplied text cites Berakhot 21b for the sorceress argument. The explicit named baraita also appears in Yevamot 4a. The next locator is abbreviated in the supplied text and the subject is carrying on Shabbat.

Sifra, Kedoshim, Chapter 4:12 and the consulted Yerushalmi Nedarim 9:4 both preserve the contrast between Akiva’s principle and Ben Azzai’s greater principle. Hyman’s printed Yerushalmi locator is 9:3.

In Bavli Chagigah 14b Ben Azzai dies and Ben Zoma is harmed. In the consulted Yerushalmi Chagigah 2:1 those outcomes are reversed. Hyman’s estimate of Ben Azzai’s age and his treatment of the competing accounts of his death remain his historical judgments.
